headline: Some Buy Telescopes. These People Build Them From Scratch.

paragraphs.text: Nearly every summer for the past 100 years, stargazers have made the bumpy trek to the top of Breezy Hill, in the woods of Springfield, Vt., to honor the age-old tradition of making telescopes by hand.

The three-day gathering, hosted by the Springfield Telescope Makers club, is called Stellafane. In the century since the club’s first convention, Stellafane has fostered a community bound by a love for the stars and a deep commitment to the craft.

The event has done more than just nurture a hobby, club members say. Stellafane has imbued generations of stargazers with skills that seeded the optics industry, contributed to cosmic discovery and influenced both space exploration and national defense. It also helped spur the rise of amateur astronomy across the globe.

But the world looks different from the way it did 100 years ago. Telescopes are widely available now and often cheaper to buy commercially than to build from scratch. Handiwork is becoming a thing of the past. Widespread light pollution has led to a loss of dark skies. Stellafane’s attendance has waned, and the club’s membership is graying.
Still, club members believe their craft, as well as the convention and community built around it, is too important to lose.

Stellafane has long served as a nucleus of “innovation and invention,” according to Douglas Arion, a club member who produced a documentary about the convention that premiered in August. “We are one of the few groups still really doing this,” he said of amateur telescope making. “And if it dies, we’re pretty much killing it off.”

Stellafane’s roots stretch back to 1920, when telescopes existed mostly in the realm of the wealthy. That began to shift when Russell Porter, largely considered the founder of the amateur telescope-making movement, gathered 16 people in a Springfield basement. He instructed them through the grinding, polishing and tuning of a chunk of glass into an atomically smooth mirror — the key component of a reflecting telescope.

The Springfield Telescope Makers was established in 1923 and completed construction of a pink clubhouse atop Breezy Hill the next year. The founders named it Stellar Fane, a phrase derived from Latin meaning “shrine to the stars.” That soon contracted to Stellafane.

Interest in telescope making exploded after Scientific American published a series of instructive articles in 1925 about the club’s activities. A handful of tinkerers congregated in 1926 on Breezy Hill, where they compared designs, shared techniques and scanned the stars with homemade telescopes. Stellafane, the convention, was born.

Attendance at what became an annual event ballooned, eventually reaching into the thousands. Over the next decades, the convention and its site earned a kind of legacy status among stargazers. “A trip to Stellafane is considered a pilgrimage,” read a 1989 form to register the club grounds as a national landmark.
The event heightened interest in observing the universe, even among those with no formal training.

“From my perspective, Stellafane ‘invented’ amateur astronomy,” Ken Slater, the webmaster of the Springfield Telescope Makers, wrote in an email. Before, most amateurs were armchair astronomers, he said. They could read about the stars, “but they could not afford a telescope to explore the night sky themselves.”

Today, a worldwide network of amateur astronomers, including many Stellafaners, monitors the sky 24/7 to observe solar system collisions; uncover new stars, comets and asteroids; contribute to eclipse science and more.

Stellafane offered one of the first venues for amateurs to connect about an otherwise solitary hobby while camping together under the stars. It also gave telescope makers a watering hole from which to perfect their techniques, which to this day can produce mirrors with a surface accuracy within a few millionths of an inch, as the random motions of grinding and polishing by human hands wash out systematic errors that can happen with machines.

Over the years, Stellafane’s annual competition also inspired imaginative ways to mount those mirrors into telescopes: Some people crafted tubes from old bicycle rims and built tripods from crutches and broken hockey sticks. In 1966, one attendee arrived with a telescope inside a hollowed-out bowling ball; ads for a strikingly similar design, available to purchase commercially, appeared a decade later.
Telescope makers also developed a suite of automated software tools — to focus their scopes, process images and the like — some of which have found their way into professional astronomy endeavors.

Inspired by their craft, many young Stellafaners went on to pursue related careers. One helped develop the optical systems on a Cold War spy plane; another did the same for an Apollo lunar landing simulator. They brought their expertise to the optics on the Keck telescopes in Hawaii and to multiple NASA missions, including the Voyagers and the James Webb Space Telescope. The corrective lenses that fixed the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 were in part crafted by an optician who passed through Stellafane.

“There’s always a time when something useful comes up and you say, ‘Oh, well, I’m familiar with that from the kind of things you learn building a telescope,’” said Mitchell Revalski, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which manages operations for the Hubble and the Webb. Dr. Revalski added that attending Stellafane as a teenager helped him finish his first scope — which now lives in a corner of his office — and largely inspired his future career as an astronomer. He is now a member of Hubble’s camera team.

Despite their reach, Stellafane and the Springfield Telescope Makers largely flew under the radar for decades to those outside of the astronomy community. Members describe the club as historically introverted. Old accounts often called the makers “telescope nuts” doing who-knows-what in the woods, a portrayal they embraced.
“It was sort of like a secret society,” Mr. Slater said.
That reputation may have hurt the club in the long run. Its current demographics skew older, white and male — evidence of a history that was not the most inclusive, club members acknowledged.
“We need to fix that,” Dr. Arion said, “for the survival of the club, for the survival of the art.”

The Springfield Telescope Makers spent more than a year strategizing for their second century as they approached the 100th anniversary of Stellafane this past August. Plans are in motion to expand the membership — currently invite-only, and requiring the completion of a telescope-worthy mirror — to include a more diverse crowd.

Some have expressed the need for more local outreach. Others are pushing for an affiliate membership class, which would allow telescope-making enthusiasts beyond New England to support the club. Katie Shusdock, a club board member who planned the convention this year, thinks that modernizing Stellafane would help attract younger people.
“It’s currently quite rustic,” said Ms. Shusdock, 29, who joined the club’s mirror-making classes at age 11. “I have big, big dreams of a showerhouse.”

Stellafane has evolved since 1926. Some 800 people attended the convention in August, and many brought with them scopes not built by hand, but purchased. They set up shop in a clearing, acquired by the club in 1986 to support the event’s expansion, east of Breezy Hill. This year’s agenda included a daylong workshop with professional astronomers, treasure hunts for children and a talk on using artificial intelligence for amateur observing.

But the heart of the event remains the same. The most dedicated attendees still spend months, even years, grinding a mirror and finding clever ways to house it in a telescope. They place their handcrafted portals to the stars in front of the pink Stellafane clubhouse and share trade secrets well into the night.
Cecilia Detrich, the president of the Springfield Telescope Makers, who is Ms. Shusdock’s mother, describes it as an “almost religious” experience.

Some makers carry on the tradition to design specialty scopes that cannot yet be found commercially. Others come because they take pride in creating something with a precision surpassing that of machines.
And then there are those who embody the truest spirit of the French word “amateur” — they craft telescopes for the love of it.
Stellafane “is more than just a location, more than just a club, more than just an annual convention,” Ms. Detrich said.

“I’m hoping that in another 100 years, people will be celebrating the bicentennial right here on Breezy Hill,” she added, “continuing to share their love of space, science, telescope making and the night sky.”
